query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high‐entropy alloys, cyclic thermal and mechanical loading can trigger stress‐induced nanocluster formation along grain boundaries that locally reduces cohesive strength, thereby initiating brittle fracture without the formation of conventional grain-boundary segregates or intermetallic phases.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially homogeneous, single‐phase, compositionally complex high‐entropy alloy with a stable microstructure and uniform grain boundary chemistry.
generation.intervention: Application of controlled thermal pre-treatments combined with cyclic mechanical (tensile or fatigue) loading designed to simulate service conditions.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant temperatures (including both moderately elevated and sub-ambient conditions) and strain rates typical of engineering applications; testing both in quasi-static and cyclic loading regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: Stress-induced formation of nanoscale compositional fluctuations or nanoclusters at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses, local driving forces overcome the high configurational entropy barrier, allowing subtle segregation into nanoscale clusters at grain boundaries. These nanoclusters reduce local grain boundary cohesion and promote brittle fracture initiation, even in the absence of precipitate formation or traditional grain-boundary segregation seen in conventional alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as-homogenized alloy, pre-treated samples will exhibit a measurable reduction in toughness and an earlier onset of brittle fracture under tensile or fatigue loading. Microstructural analysis is expected to reveal the presence of nano-scale clusters at grain boundaries without evidence of large-scale segregation or intermetallic precipitation.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or homogenized single-phase high-entropy alloy exhibiting uniformly high ductility and toughness.
generation.boundary: Effects are expected within service temperature regimes where the alloy remains a single phase (i.e., no macroscopic phase separation) and under mechanical strain rates relevant for structural applications.
generation.uncertainty: The exact extent and kinetics of nanocluster formation, and its quantitative effect on toughness reduction, remain uncertain due to limits in microanalytical resolution and potential variations across alloy compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of high-entropy alloy specimens: one maintained in the baseline homogenized state and the other subjected to controlled cyclic thermal and mechanical loading designed to simulate long-term service conditions. Perform tensile and fatigue tests over a range of temperatures. Concurrently, use high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to assess the presence of nanoclusters along grain boundaries.
measurements: Fatigue life and crack initiation data under cyclic loading
High-resolution TEM/EDS analysis of grain boundary chemistry and structure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally and mechanically cycled specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction in fracture toughness relative to the baseline, or if microstructural analysis fails to detect any unique nanocluster formation (with brittle failure instead correlating with conventional segregation or precipitation), then the proposed mechanism of stress‐induced nanocluster mediated brittle behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The presence of intermetallic compounds, such as brittle Laves phases, typically reduces the ductility of RHEAs (), prompting extensive efforts to develop single-phase RHEAs for high-temperature applications (, , , , , , ). The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta also exhibits impressive tensile ductility, ~14% at room temperature (), and a relatively low brittle-to-ductile transition temperature between −47° and −27°C, comparable to BCC metals and stainless steels for engineering applications (, ). In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions.
